newsitem.title: JAPAN: Kabun Muto a "lone wolf" in Japan government.
newsitem.headline: Kabun Muto a "lone wolf" in Japan government.

text.p: Kabun Muto, whose remarks sparked turmoil in financial markets this week, is regarded as a senior figure but something of a lone wolf within Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto's government,

Political analysts said that Muto, director-general of the Management and Coordination Agency and a senior figure in the ruling Liberal Democratic Party (LDP), feels free to speak his mind but does not necessarily reflect government thinking. The agency is in charge of helping to shrink Japan's huge government bureaucracy.
"If I dare to characterise Muto, I would say he is a lone wolf who freely says what he wants to say," leading political analyst Minoru Morita said.
"Muto is not close to Prime Minister Hashimoto," he said.
The 69-year-old Muto said on Friday that any "artificial" attempt to check a further decline in the yen could fail in the current environment of a continuing capital outflow from Japan.
He said that there was nothing wrong with the dollar moving above 125 yen, adding that, in terms of purchasing power, 150 yen to the dollar would be an appropriate level.
His remarks sparked a near-instant denial from the powerful Ministry of Finance, which said the statements did not reflect official government policy.

On Tuesday, Muto said he had asked Bank of Japan Governor Yasuo Matsushita to consider the possibility of raising the nation's key interest rate, the official discount rate, which the central bank charges on overnight loans to commercial banks.
Morita said Muto's remarks showed that the Hashimoto government was in some confusion.
"The fact that Muto has made such remarks at his discretion means that the Hashimoto administration is not monolithic at all. I would say it's in disarray," Morita said.
He noted that many Japanese, especially the elderly, are upset with Japan's record-low interest rates.
"In that sense, his remarks are very political and targetted at voters in his constituency, not the world financial markets," he added.
Muto, elected to the powerful Lower House of parliament 11 times, had served as ministers of foreign affairs, agriculture and trade.
During 1993 general elections, Muto came under fire from party colleagues for saying: "If Prime Minister (Kiichi) Miyazawa died, the LDP would score a landslide victory".
